newsitem.title: USA: Barney's to close stores in cost-cutting plan.
newsitem.headline: Barney's to close stores in cost-cutting plan.

text.p: Bankrupt retailer Barney's Inc. said Tuesday it would close several underperforming stores, including its famed downtown Manhattan location, as part of a cost-cutting plan.
The move is the latest setback for the upscale retailer, which is mired in lawsuits with a former Japanese business partner and is seeking help from an outside investor.

The parent of Barneys New York said it also would close stores in Dallas and Houston, as well as in Troy, Mich. It will cut costs at its New York headquarters and at its Lyndhurst, N.J., distribution centre.
Company President John Brincko said the company had no choice but to close the stores because they were performing poorly.

The privately held company said it will continue to operate three major stores in New York, Chicago and Beverly Hills; five regional stores and a smaller store at the World Financial Centre in New York City as well as 10 outlet stores throughout the country.
The Manhattan store at Seventh Avenue and 17th Street is expected to close in September, while the others will be closed by the end of July, the company said.
Brincko said many employees affected will be offered positions at the remaining stores.

With the closures and other cost cutting, Barney's will employ about 1,750 workers in nine stores in New York City and Manhasset, N.Y.; Beverly Hills and Costa Mesa, Calif.; Chicago; Chestnut Hills, Mass.; Westport, Conn., and Seattle.
The number will also include those retained at the 10 outlets and the New Jersey distribution site.

Founded in 1923 by Barney Pressman and operated by grandsons Robert and Gene, the company has been plagued by a reputation for weak management and criticised for pouring too much money into expansion, most notably at its store on Manhattan's pricey Madison Avenue that competes with exclusive boutiques run by top French and American apparel designers.
Although Barney's has shuffled management to help turn around its troubled operations, it has long been viewed as a weak performer in the luxury retail sector even as other companies do well.

But Brincko was positive on the company's outlook, saying earnings of the Barney's chain "significantly improved" recently and the closings as well as other cost-cutting efforts will speed up such improvement.
"Our reorganization strategy is proceeding on a timely, positive track," he said.
Meanwhile, potential investors are expected to submit plans by July 7 and the company is expected to respond by July 25.
The company has received a $240 million bid from Hong Kong retailer Dickson Concepts Ltd., but the company's creditors have rejected the offer as too low.
Barney's former business partner, Isetan Co Ltd., has teamed up with Saks Holdings Inc. with a bid of about $290 million.
Upscale retailers Neiman Marcus Group Inc. and Canada's Holt Renfrew & Co. Ltd. also reportedly have expressed interest.
A spokeswoman for Saks declined to comment on the store closings. Officials from Dickson and Isetan could not immediately be reached for comment.
A lawyer representing Barney's creditors said the move to close stores is a solid decision to protect the company in case a sale falls apart.
"The committee is very anxious to pursue the sale process," said Robert Raskin of law firm Stroock & Stroock & Lavan LLP.
One Wall Street analyst said the store closings would likely be viewed positively by potential buyers.

"If they're money-losing stores, they probably would have been closed anyway, either now or after an acquisition. It's something they need to do whether they're being bought out or whether they stay independent," said William Armstrong of Fahnestock & Co.
